method: Points are read in order, one latitude, longitude and elevation per line, in decimal degrees and metres. Consecutive points are joined with the haversine great-circle distance on a sphere of radius 6,371 km, and the route distance is the sum of those legs; each point is also placed on the profile at its running distance from the start. Ascent and descent use a hysteresis filter: the elevation change from the last counted turning point is only accumulated once it reaches the ignore threshold, and the turning point then moves to the current sample, so changes smaller than the threshold never accumulate. A threshold of 0 counts every metre, an empty threshold is treated as 0, and a larger threshold therefore reports less climbing for the same noisy track. Steepest climb and descent are taken over individual legs that are at least 20 m long, because a few metres between dense samples turns centimetre elevation noise into huge percentages; a route whose legs are all shorter than that reports no grade, and legs between identical coordinates contribute no distance and are skipped. Net change is the last elevation minus the first, the elevation range is the highest sample minus the lowest, and ascent per kilometre divides the total climb by the route length, so it is undefined for a zero-length route. Distances are reported in kilometres and miles and elevations in metres and feet. Worked default: the eight sample points of the ridge route span 3,011 m, climb 225 m in four counted rises, descend 87 m in three counted drops, and end 138 m above the start, with a 13.5% steepest climb and a 15.0% steepest descent. Limits: two to 2000 points, latitude from -90 to 90 degrees, longitude from -180 to 180 degrees, elevation from -500 to 9000 metres and a smoothing threshold from 0 to 100 metres; a missing, malformed or out-of-range value is rejected with the offending line number rather than defaulted. The model assumes a spherical Earth, straight legs between samples and trustworthy elevations: it does not correct for ellipsoidal geodesy, barometric drift, missing samples, switchbacks that double back within one leg, or gradient over a smoothed window. Calculations run entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: Leg distance is the haversine great-circle distance on a 6,371 km sphere, and route distance is the sum of the legs.
Ascent and descent accumulate only changes that reach the ignore threshold, then reset the reference elevation to that sample.
Steepest climb and descent are the largest signed gain over leg distance, over legs at least 20 m long.
Profile points are placed at cumulative distance with elevation scaled between the lowest and highest sample.
